A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers:
How Language Models Forget Their Prompt

Shuyang Xiang Affiliation: Independent researcher
October 2026
Abstract

A black hole retains only a few conserved charges of the matter it formed from. We ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating tt tokens. Consider two different prompts followed by the same continuation text, so that any difference in their hidden states comes from the prompt alone, and we find that the distance between their hidden states decays approximately as a power law t−αt^{-\alpha}, where α=1\alpha=1 is the rate at which a fixed prompt’s share of uniform attention shrinks and smaller values mean longer memory. Beyond the first layers, trained models forget fast (α≈0.55\alpha\approx 0.55–0.70.7), while untrained models with the same architecture forget slowly (α≈0.2\alpha\approx 0.2–0.50.5, decreasing with depth). We prove that this offset is O⁡(P​(log⁡t)L−1/t)O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big) for a prompt of length PP and depth LL. The bound holds for finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with full causal attention and bounded attention logits (e.g. rotary position encodings), under one additional condition: the pre-norm activations stay away from zero. The mechanism is geometric: the prompt’s direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and relay — continuation tokens passing on what earlier tokens read from the prompt — can only add logarithmic factors. This is what we call the conditional no-hair theorem: given the text generated so far, the prompt’s influence on the next token vanishes as tt grows, so any property of the prompt that survives, such as its language, must be carried by the text itself. An exactly solvable linear relay model shows that the bound cannot be improved and reproduces the rise of the local exponent towards 11 seen in untrained networks. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias on the prompt stops the decay early in training and makes the offset grow after training, so dilution is necessary for the forgetting we measure; untrained networks and the solvable model show that it is also sufficient. An attention path decomposition shows that training suppresses relay within the first billion tokens, before attention sinks form. A mild version of this compensation tends to raise adherence to system instructions at a small perplexity cost, though no more than a constant boost of equal mean strength. We will release the toolkit used in this paper, which measures α\alpha for any Hugging Face causal language model.

1 Introduction

Think of a conversation that runs long with your friends. You open with a remark about the weather — Wednesday looks nice, say, or Thursday looks nice — and by the time it has moved through work, a film, a friend’s illness, nobody could tell from the last ten minutes which of the two you said. The opening line is still in the room, in the sense that nothing was deleted. It has simply stopped mattering. Large language models behave the same way. A system prompt sits at the start of the context, all of its tokens visible to every later query, and yet over a few dialogue turns the persona it sets drifts measurably (Li et al., 2024). An agent whose constraints are given once, at the start of a long trajectory, undergoes the same erosion. Nothing is truncated, and still the model stops listening. We ask how fast this erosion occurs, and what drives it. We find that the decay is close to a power law, and that — counterintuitively — the training process itself accelerates this amnesia, causing a trained network to forget earlier constraints faster than a random-weight baseline. Whatever information does persist, such as the language of the prompt, survives not because the network retains a memory of the past, but because that past has already been inscribed into the local geometry of the generated text.

Why should an opening remark fade at all, when it never leaves the context? Physics offers a template. A black hole forgets almost everything about the matter that formed it: an exterior observer can only measure a few charges, and these persist because the exterior field itself can carry them. The corresponding questions for a transformer are then clear.

The core inquiry of this paper is simple to state. Give a language model a prompt, let it write tt tokens, and compare two prompts that differ in a single word, in phrasing, in language, or in genre. Long after the prompt, can anything inside the model still tell them apart? And if not, why not?

We call the residual amount of the prompt in the hidden state its imprint, and ask three questions about it: how large is the imprint after tt generated tokens, how fast does it decay, and what properties of the prompt can still be read off from it. Whether an imprint of a given size is readable depends on how it compares with the variation that the continuation itself causes, so we also track a decodability ratio: the imprint measured against the spread of hidden states across different continuations. The two quantities are not the same, but they are linked — a decoder can read the prompt off the state only while the imprint stands out against the continuation — and we show in what follows that in practice they decay at the same rate, which lets a single exponent summarise how quickly a prompt is forgotten.

This paper answers these questions in three steps. We first define a quantity that can be measured: the prompt offset, the difference between the hidden states of two runs that share a continuation but differ in their prompt. We then prove that, under mild conditions on the architecture, this offset decays at least as fast as t−1t^{-1} up to logarithmic factors, and show that the bound is attained by a model that can be solved exactly. Finally, we trace where the prompt’s influence goes as it decays: through the attention path we call relay, which the training process suppresses within the first billion tokens.

Contributions.

The imprint is measured as a prompt offset, and five results characterise how it decays.

  1. 1.

    The measured decay. We define the teacher-forced prompt offset and show that it decays approximately as t−αt^{-\alpha}, with logarithmic corrections in untrained networks and close to a pure power law in trained Pythia on coherent text. The spread across continuations stays essentially constant (β≈0\beta\approx 0 except in untrained Qwen), so the rate at which the prompt is forgotten is governed by a single exponent (Section 3).

  2. 2.

    A theoretical bound. For finite-depth pre-LN transformers with non-degenerate pre-norm activations, the offset is O⁡(P​(log⁡t)L−1/t)O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big); conditional on the generated text, the prompt’s influence on the next token vanishes at the same rate. Uniform attention attains the bound asymptotically, and the resulting linear relay model is solved exactly for arbitrary layer gains (Section 4).

  3. 3.

    The relay mechanism. We decompose the attention contribution to the offset into a direct path (queries reading the prompt) and a relay path (queries reading continuation tokens that already carry prompt information). The decomposition reproduces the measured α\alpha within 0.060.06 at every layer and training stage (Section 6).

  4. 4.

    From mechanism to training. Compensating the dilution with a logit bias on the prompt removes or reverses forgetting; on Pythia, forgetting appears within the first billion training tokens, before attention sinks form; attention weights alone are a misleading proxy (Sections 6.2 and 7).

  5. 5.

    An application, with its costs. A mild log⁡t\log t compensation increases instruction adherence at a small perplexity cost but induces instruction echoing; in multi-turn conversations it shows a consistent trend towards higher adherence, but no more than a constant boost with the same mean bias, so the benefit comes from extra attention to the instruction rather than from the shape of the compensation (Section 9).

2 Related work

Where this paper sits.

Three lines of work are close to ours. One studies the practical failure of long contexts: instruction drift, attention sinks, and the limits of what a model can generate. The second studies information flow through attention, both empirically and as over-squashing. The third studies the statistical structure of long text and the power-law decay of attention. Our question “how much of a prompt remains in the hidden state after tt generated tokens?” sits between these lines, and our answer borrows from each: the failure mode is from the first, the path decomposition from the second, the power law from the third.

Instruction drift.

Li et al. (2024) show that adherence to a system prompt degrades within a few dialogue rounds, attribute it to attention decay, and propose split-softmax. Our causal experiment agrees on the cause, and our quantitative law explains why the drift occurs: the prompt’s share of attention shrinks as 1/t1/t under uniform attention, so the decay is a geometric consequence of a growing context rather than an artefact of any particular dialogue pattern.

Attention sinks and over-mixing.

Sinks absorb attention without carrying information (Xiao et al., 2024; Gu and others, 2025); Barbero and others (2025) argue that they prevent over-mixing. Our relay path is a form of mixing, and our training-dynamics measurement settles the ordering: the onset of forgetting precedes sink formation by several billion tokens, so sinks cannot be its initial cause.

Information flow.

Norm-based attention analysis (Kobayashi et al., 2020) and attention flow (Abnar and Zuidema, 2020) motivate our path decomposition; rank collapse (Dong et al., 2021) is a depth-wise counterpart of the token-wise mixing studied here. Barbero et al. (2024) show that in decoder-only transformers the sensitivity of the last token to earlier tokens is limited by over-squashing; our theorem makes this loss quantitative for a fixed prompt as generation proceeds, and the linear relay model shows that the t−1t^{-1} rate cannot be improved in the uniform-attention regime.

Long-range statistics of text.

Mutual information in natural text decays as a power law (Lin and Tegmark, 2017; Chen et al., 2025). A power-law forgetting curve could in principle be inherited from the data. Our random-initialisation baseline rules this out for the existence of the power law: an untrained network, whose weights carry no statistics of any corpus, already forgets as a power law, with exponents that are unchanged (to within 0.010.01) when the continuation sentences are shuffled. In trained networks the exponent does depend on the continuation text (Section 5.5), but the ordering of the axes and the trained–untrained contrast do not.

Prompt influence on generated text.

Marklová et al. (2026) rescore a fixed generation under different prompts and find that the influence of the prompt fades with accumulated context. Where they measure the effect on the output distribution, we measure it on the hidden state, which lets us track its decay layer by layer and separate the direct path from relay.

Power-law decay of attention.

Attention scores to earlier tokens are known to decay roughly as a power law over generation steps, which Koley et al. (2025) exploit for dynamic sparse attention. Our dilution lemma gives a mechanism for such decay; the path decomposition shows, however, that attention weights are an unreliable proxy for information flow, because sinks attract weight without carrying prompt-specific content, and the decay of the trace in the hidden state is what determines whether the prompt is still readable.

Limits of long generation.

Meyer et al. (2026) bound which output sequences a transformer can generate at all, finding a sharp length threshold beyond which most sequences become inaccessible. Their question is what a model can produce; ours is the complementary one of how the influence of a given prompt on what it produces decays.

Attention fading and length-dependent scaling.

Nakanishi (2025) observes that softmax attention flattens as the context grows (“attention fading”) and proposes Scalable-Softmax, which multiplies the logits by s​log⁡ns\log n. Our dilution lemma is a quantitative form of the same effect. A logit scaling that grows with context length makes the logits unbounded, so Lemma 1(a) and with it Lemma 2 no longer apply (see the scope paragraph in Appendix A); our analysis therefore predicts that such scalings, including Scalable-Softmax, retain prompt information longer.

3 Setup and measurement

We want to know whether a model that has generated tt tokens after a prompt still carries that prompt in its hidden state, and how fast this memory fades as tt grows. Answering it requires three choices: what to compare, so that a difference in hidden states can only come from the prompt (Section 3.1); what to measure, so that the result says whether the prompt can be read off the state (Section 3.2); and how to estimate decay rates reliably (Section 3.3).

3.1 What to compare

Let a decoder-only language model receive a prompt xx of PP tokens and then generate autoregressively, without further input. After tt generated tokens, information about xx can be held in two places. The first is the generated text, which any observer can read: call this the exterior. The second is the residual stream at the current position, which also sees xx through attention: call this the interior. Only the interior is a memory of the network; the exterior is a record anyone could consult. This distinction is the same one that separates a black hole from its exterior field, and it will return when we ask what survives.

The natural experiment, letting two prompts generate freely and comparing their hidden states, cannot tell these apart: two prompts produce two different texts, and a difference in hidden states may be a memory of the prompt or merely a response to different text. We therefore fix the text: both prompts are followed by the same continuation cc, written independently of either, and we compare the hidden states along it. With the continuation held fixed, any remaining difference between the two runs must come from the prompt. This is also the quantity bounded by Theorem 1, and the one that must vanish for a no-hair statement to hold.

The measurements in this section and in Sections 4–9 therefore use what we call teacher-forcing: the continuation is written by a human, not by the model. This is a measurement device, not the failure mode itself. The failure mode is the one that occurs in free generation, when the continuation is produced by the model and the prompt’s influence can only travel through the text it has caused; Section 8 returns to that setting and asks what survives.

3.2 What to measure

The most direct imprint of the prompt is the difference between the two hidden states. Fix a layer ll, and let hl​(x∘c,t)∈ℝdh_{l}(x\circ c,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the residual stream after block ll (before normalisation) at time tt along cc, where dd is the hidden dimension and ∘\circ denotes concatenation, so that x∘cx\circ c is the prompt followed by the continuation. To reduce token-level fluctuations we average it over a fixed window of consecutive continuation tokens and assign it the time tt of the window’s centre.

Definition 1 (Prompt offset).

For two prompts x,x′x,x^{\prime} and a shared continuation cc, the prompt offset at layer ll and time tt is

Δl​(t,c)=hl​(x′∘c,t)−hl​(x∘c,t),with norm ​δl​(t,c)=‖Δl​(t,c)‖.\Delta_{l}(t;c)=h_{l}(x^{\prime}\circ c,t)-h_{l}(x\circ c,t),\qquad\text{with norm }\delta_{l}(t;c)=\|\Delta_{l}(t;c)\|.

We write Δl,j\Delta_{l,j} for the jj-th coordinate of Δl\Delta_{l}, and hl,jh_{l,j} for the jj-th coordinate of hlh_{l}.

A small offset is not by itself evidence of forgetting: what matters is whether it stands out against the variation that the continuation itself causes. If the offset is the same for every continuation, the prompt can be read off the state whatever text follows; if it is swamped by the differences between continuations, it cannot. We therefore split the offset into a part common to all continuations, the signal, and compare it with the spread of hidden states across continuations, the noise. Both are measured in units of σl,j\sigma_{l,j}, the standard deviation of hl,jh_{l,j} across continuations in the first window, pooled over both prompts, so that no coordinate dominates because of its scale. We write ncn_{c} for the number of continuations per pair, and 𝔼c\mathbb{E}_{c} and Varc\operatorname{Var}_{c} for the mean and variance across them.

Definition 2 (Signal, noise and decay exponents).

The signal and the noise at layer ll are

𝒮l​(t)=1d​∑j=1d(𝔼c​Δl,j​(t,c))2σl,j2,𝒩l​(t)=1d​∑j=1dVarc⁡hl,j​(x∘c,t)σl,j2,\mathcal{S}_{l}(t)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\big(\mathbb{E}_{c}\,\Delta_{l,j}(t;c)\big)^{2}}{\sigma_{l,j}^{2}},\qquad\mathcal{N}_{l}(t)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{c}\,h_{l,j}(x\circ c,t)}{\sigma_{l,j}^{2}}, (1)

and we summarise how fast each decays by a power-law exponent: 𝒮l​(t)∝t−2​αl\mathcal{S}_{l}(t)\propto t^{-2\alpha_{l}} and 𝒩l​(t)∝t−2​βl\mathcal{N}_{l}(t)\propto t^{-2\beta_{l}}.

The exponent we care about is αl\alpha_{l}: it measures how quickly the signal of the prompt fades. The exponent βl\beta_{l} measures how quickly the noise fades as well, and we track it because a prompt is only decodable while the signal stands out against the noise: decodability scales as t−2​(αl−βl)t^{-2(\alpha_{l}-\beta_{l})}. We find βl≈0\beta_{l}\approx 0 almost everywhere (Section 5), so the rate at which the prompt is forgotten is the single number αl\alpha_{l}.

3.3 Estimating decay rates

Sampling times.

Decay laws are best seen on a logarithmic time axis, so we space measurements by octaves. For Pythia on real-corpus pairs, windows end at te=16,32,…,1024t_{e}=16,32,\dots,1024; for Qwen, at te=16,…,2048t_{e}=16,\dots,2048. For the hand-written scenes, which use Pythia and whose continuations are at least 19201920 tokens long, the same octave spacing runs to te=1920t_{e}=1920, short of Pythia’s 20482048-token context. Each window covers the 1616 tokens ending at these points. We label it by its centre, not by its end: end labelling biases the fitted exponent upwards when a window spans a whole octave, as it does in the first octaves. For offsets of the form (P+s)−α(P+s)^{-\alpha}, the bias is up to 0.190.19 locally and 0.070.07 globally with end labels, against less than 0.030.03 and 0.010.01 with centre labels; on our data the global exponents drop by 0.050.05–0.100.10 when going from end to centre labels.

Signal.

The signal is the part of the offset common to all continuations, so we estimate it by averaging Δl,j\Delta_{l,j} over continuations and squaring. At late times this average is small, and the naive estimate (𝔼c​Δl,j)2(\mathbb{E}_{c}\Delta_{l,j})^{2} is then dominated by its sampling bias Varc⁡Δl,j/nc\operatorname{Var}_{c}\Delta_{l,j}/n_{c}, which would make the decay look slower than it is. We therefore use the unbiased estimator

𝒮^l​(t)=1d​nc​(nc−1)​∑a≠b∑j=1dΔl,j​(t,ca)​Δl,j​(t,cb)σl,j2,\widehat{\mathcal{S}}_{l}(t)=\frac{1}{d\,n_{c}(n_{c}-1)}\sum_{a\neq b}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\Delta_{l,j}(t;c_{a})\,\Delta_{l,j}(t;c_{b})}{\sigma_{l,j}^{2}},

which corrects for this bias by averaging over pairs of continuations rather than squaring the mean. We also report the exponent of the mean squared offset ℳl​(t)=1d​∑j𝔼c​Δl,j2/σl,j2\mathcal{M}_{l}(t)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j}\mathbb{E}_{c}\Delta_{l,j}^{2}/\sigma_{l,j}^{2}. Unlike 𝒮l\mathcal{S}_{l}, which averages the offset before squaring and therefore cancels offsets whose direction varies across continuations, ℳl\mathcal{M}_{l} averages the squared offset, so it captures both the common part and the variation in direction. Comparing the two tells us how much of the decay is decorrelation rather than shrinking norm (Remark 2).

We use nc=8n_{c}=8 continuations per pair for real-corpus pairs and nc=16n_{c}=16 per scene for hand-written scenes. All real-corpus exponents of Section 5 use 𝒮^\widehat{\mathcal{S}}, and so do the path decomposition (Section 6), the compensation experiment (Section 7) and the trade-off (Section 9). The hand-written scenes use the plug-in estimate, because the correction requires storing pairwise products of offsets, which the earlier runs did not record; their late-time exponents are correspondingly biased low.

Exponents.

The signal is first averaged over prompt pairs (and, where stated, over axes); the global exponent αl\alpha_{l} is the least-squares slope of −12​ln⁡𝒮^l-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\widehat{\mathcal{S}}_{l} against ln⁡t\ln t over all measurement points, with 95%95\% bootstrap intervals over scenes or prompt pairs. A single exponent can hide a decay that is not a pure power law, so we also compute the local exponent αloc\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}, the same slope between consecutive points. A pure power law has constant αloc\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}; dilution with logarithmic corrections gives an αloc\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}} that rises towards 11 (Section 4). βl\beta_{l} is estimated in the same way from 𝒩l\mathcal{N}_{l}.

3.4 Prompts and continuations

Our picture predicts that the decay exponent α\alpha depends on the architecture and on the length of the prompt, but not on how different the two prompts are: a larger difference should raise the amplitude of the offset, not change how fast it decays. We test this prediction by varying the kind and size of the difference, on two sets of prompts.

Hand-written scenes.

Twenty scenes, each with a base prompt and four variants, from the smallest to the largest change: one content word changed (detail), a paraphrase (para), a news-wire rewrite (genre) and a translation (lang). Continuations are human-written: sixteen passages per scene from the WikiText-103 validation set, at least 19201920 tokens long, shared by all five prompts of the scene. The full list is in Appendix C.

Real-corpus pairs.

Hand-written prompts may share stylistic regularities, so we repeat the measurement on pairs drawn from public corpora, one hundred per axis: a WikiText sentence and the same sentence with one word replaced (detail), MRPC paraphrase pairs (para), WMT14 English–French pairs (lang), and two unrelated WikiText sentences (unrelated), the largest possible difference. Continuations are passages from the WikiText-103 validation set, eight per pair, shared by both prompts of the pair.

Shared first token.

Trained models often concentrate attention on the first token, an attention sink (Xiao et al., 2024). When two prompts begin with different tokens, the sink itself differs, and its contribution need not dilute. Where stated, we prepend a common token (<|endoftext|>) to both prompts to remove this difference.

3.5 Models

Two questions guide the choice of models: when during training does the forgetting rate change, and does the picture depend on architectural details? Pythia (Biderman and others, 2023) answers the first, since it provides training checkpoints of a fixed architecture (LayerNorm, parallel residual): we use Pythia-160m at eight checkpoints from initialisation to the end of training (steps 00, 128128, 256256, 512512, 10001000, 40004000, 1600016000, 143000143000), and Pythia-410m and Pythia-1b at initialisation and after training, to separate the effects of training, width and depth. Qwen2.5 (Qwen Team, 2025) addresses the second with a different architecture (RMSNorm, sequential residual, grouped-query attention): we use Qwen2.5-0.5B, trained and at random initialisation (the library’s default scheme: normal weights with standard deviation 0.020.02, seed 00; for Pythia, step 00 is the released initial checkpoint), and the trained Qwen2.5-1.5B. All computations run in float32 on a single Apple-silicon laptop.

4 A conditional no-hair theorem

4.1 Setting and notation

Architecture.

We work with LL-layer pre-LN decoders: causal attention, residual connections, and rotary or no positional encoding inside the logits (as in Pythia and Qwen). The pre-LN placement matters here: each block normalises its input inside the residual branch, before attention and before the MLP, so the residual stream itself is never normalised. This is the sequential form, hl=hl−1+Attn⁡(LN⁡(hl−1))h_{l}=h_{l-1}+\mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{LN}(h_{l-1})) followed by the MLP update, as in Qwen, or the parallel form, where both updates are computed from hl−1h_{l-1} and added, as in Pythia. The scope covers most current decoders, with LayerNorm or RMSNorm (see below); it excludes post-LN blocks, linear attention and recurrent state.

Notation.

We use the same setup as Section 3, with one change of notation for the proof. Two prompts x,x′x,x^{\prime} are followed by the same continuation cc, and hl​(i)h_{l}(i), hl′​(i)h^{\prime}_{l}(i) denote the residual streams at the ii-th continuation token after ll blocks. This is the quantity hl​(x∘c,t)h_{l}(x\circ c,t) of Definition 1, with the time index tt replaced by the distance ii from the end of the prompt. Write δl​(i)=‖hl​(i)−hl′​(i)‖\delta_{l}(i)=\|h_{l}(i)-h^{\prime}_{l}(i)\|. Token embeddings of the continuation coincide, so δ0​(i)=0\delta_{0}(i)=0.

The two prompts have lengths PP and P′P^{\prime}. From here on, PP denotes the larger of the two, so that any bound in terms of PP applies to both. We index continuation positions by their distance i≥1i\geq 1 from the end of the prompt, so the ii-th continuation query attends to at most P+iP+i keys. With rotary encodings, positions enter only the logits, through relative offsets, so P≠P′P\neq P^{\prime} is allowed; with absolute position embeddings we take P=P′P=P^{\prime}.

Finally, we write the normalisation as LN⁡(h)=d​Π​h/‖Π​h‖\mathrm{LN}(h)=\sqrt{d}\,\Pi h/\|\Pi h\|. Here 𝟏\mathbf{1} is the all-ones vector, II the identity, and Π=I−1d​1 1⊤\Pi=I-\tfrac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\,\mathbf{1}^{\top} the projection onto the subspace orthogonal to it, so that Π​h=h−h¯​ 1\Pi h=h-\bar{h}\,\mathbf{1} with h¯\bar{h} the mean of hh. Thus LN\mathrm{LN} first removes the mean and then rescales to length d\sqrt{d}. The gain and bias of the layer are absorbed into the adjacent linear maps and do not appear separately. RMSNorm is the special case Π=I\Pi=I, in which the mean is not removed.

The proof needs the normalisation layers to be well conditioned:

Assumption 1 (Non-degenerate pre-norm activations).

There is r>0r>0 such that ‖Π​h‖≥r\|\Pi h\|\geq r at every position and in both runs, whenever hh is the input of blocks 2,…,L2,\dots,L, the input of the final norm, or, in a sequential block, the post-attention residual that the MLP reads.

The assumption is what gives the normalisation Lipschitz: the constant in Lemma 1 is 2​d/r2\sqrt{d}/r, and it degenerates if Π​h\Pi h can vanish. In a pre-LN residual stream it cannot do so in a harmful way. The stream is never normalised, and each block adds its update to it, so the norm grows with depth rather than collapsing; the only vectors that come close to the degenerate case are the token embeddings, which are excluded from the assumption. On the sequences we measured (up to 10241024 continuation tokens), the assumption holds at block inputs with a comfortable margin: r/d=0.11r/\sqrt{d}=0.11 (Pythia-160m, initialisation), 0.240.24 (160m, trained), 0.490.49 (1b, trained) and 0.1050.105 (Qwen2.5-0.5B), against medians of order 0.10.1–44 (Appendix B). Qwen’s blocks are sequential, so the input of the post-attention norm enters as well; its minimum is 0.0120.012 in the first block of the trained model and 0.140.14 or more in all later blocks. For Qwen2.5-0.5B the constant of Assumption 1 is therefore r/d=0.012r/\sqrt{d}=0.012, set by this first post-attention norm: the assumption holds, with a small margin in that block only. These checks are empirical: they cover the measured sequences and lengths and do not establish the assumption for arbitrary continuations or contexts. All other constants follow from the weights.

4.2 Dilution

Theorem 1 rests on one geometric fact. A prompt of length PP occupies a fixed number of positions, while a query at distance ii sees P+iP+i keys; as ii grows, the prompt’s share of the query’s attention can only shrink. This is what we call dilution. We write si​js_{ij} for the logit of query ii against key jj, so that the attention weights are ai​j=esi​j/∑kesi​ka_{ij}=e^{s_{ij}}/\sum_{k}e^{s_{ik}}. We first collect the constants that the architecture imposes (Lemma 1), then make dilution precise (Lemma 2), and finally turn it into a recursion across layers (Lemma 3).

Lemma 1 (Consequences of the architecture).

Let ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denote spectral norms of the weight matrices and dhd_{h} the head dimension.

  1. (a)

    Bounded logits, unconditionally: |si​j|≤B:=d​‖WQ‖​‖WK‖/dh|s_{ij}|\leq B:=d\,\|W_{Q}\|\|W_{K}\|/\sqrt{d_{h}} (plus bias terms), since ‖LN⁡(h)‖=d\|\mathrm{LN}(h)\|=\sqrt{d} and rotary matrices are orthogonal.

  2. (b)

    LayerNorm is Lipschitz away from zero: under Assumption 1, ‖LN⁡(h)−LN⁡(h′)‖≤(2​d/r)​‖h−h′‖\|\mathrm{LN}(h)-\mathrm{LN}(h^{\prime})\|\leq(2\sqrt{d}/r)\,\|h-h^{\prime}\|.

  3. (c)

    Hence value-output vectors are bounded by V:=d​‖WO​WV‖V:=\sqrt{d}\,\|W_{O}W_{V}\| and ρ\rho-Lipschitz with ρ:=2​d​‖WO​WV‖/r\rho:=2\sqrt{d}\,\|W_{O}W_{V}\|/r; logits are λ\lambda-Lipschitz in each argument with λ:=2​d​‖WQ‖​‖WK‖/(r​dh)\lambda:=2d\,\|W_{Q}\|\|W_{K}\|/(r\sqrt{d_{h}}); the MLP update is μ\mu-Lipschitz with μ:=Lip⁡(σ)​‖W2‖​‖W1‖​ 2​d/r\mu:=\mathrm{Lip}(\sigma)\|W_{2}\|\|W_{1}\|\,2\sqrt{d}/r, where σ\sigma is the MLP nonlinearity, W1,W2W_{1},W_{2} its weight matrices and Lip⁡(σ)\mathrm{Lip}(\sigma) its Lipschitz constant.

Proof.

(a) The logit is si​j=⟨WQ​LN​(hi),WK​LN​(hj)⟩/dhs_{ij}=\langle W_{Q}\mathrm{LN}(h_{i}),W_{K}\mathrm{LN}(h_{j})\rangle/\sqrt{d_{h}}. By Cauchy–Schwarz, we have: |si​j|≤‖WQ‖​‖LN⁡(hi)‖|WK|‖LN⁡(hj)‖/dh|s_{ij}|\leq\|W_{Q}\|\,\|\mathrm{LN}(h_{i})\|\,\|W_{K}\|\,\|\mathrm{LN}(h_{j})\|/\sqrt{d_{h}}. Since ‖LN⁡(h)‖=d\|\mathrm{LN}(h)\|=\sqrt{d} and rotary matrices are orthogonal, this gives |si​j|≤d​‖WQ‖​‖WK‖/dh|s_{ij}|\leq d\,\|W_{Q}\|\|W_{K}\|/\sqrt{d_{h}}.

(b) Π\Pi is an orthogonal projection, hence non-expansive, so ‖Π​u−Π​v‖≤‖u−v‖\|\Pi u-\Pi v\|\leq\|u-v\|. For ‖u‖,‖v‖≥r\|u\|,\|v\|\geq r,

‖Π​u‖Π​u‖−Π​v‖Π​v‖‖≤‖Π​u−Π​v‖‖Π​u‖+‖Π​v‖​|1‖Π​u‖−1‖Π​v‖|≤‖Π​u−Π​v‖+|‖Π​v‖−‖Π​u‖|r≤2​‖u−v‖r,\Big\|\frac{\Pi u}{\|\Pi u\|}-\frac{\Pi v}{\|\Pi v\|}\Big\|\leq\frac{\|\Pi u-\Pi v\|}{\|\Pi u\|}+\|\Pi v\|\Big|\frac{1}{\|\Pi u\|}-\frac{1}{\|\Pi v\|}\Big|\leq\frac{\|\Pi u-\Pi v\|+|\|\Pi v\|-\|\Pi u\||}{r}\leq\frac{2\|u-v\|}{r},

using ‖Π​u‖,‖Π​v‖≥r\|\Pi u\|,\|\Pi v\|\geq r in the second step and |‖Π​v‖−‖Π​u‖|≤‖Π​u−Π​v‖≤‖u−v‖\big|\|\Pi v\|-\|\Pi u\|\big|\leq\|\Pi u-\Pi v\|\leq\|u-v\| in the last.

(c) The value-output vector WO​WV​LN​(hj)W_{O}W_{V}\mathrm{LN}(h_{j}) has norm at most d​‖WO​WV‖=V\sqrt{d}\,\|W_{O}W_{V}\|=V, and is ρ\rho-Lipschitz with ρ=2​d​‖WO​WV‖/r\rho=2\sqrt{d}\,\|W_{O}W_{V}\|/r, by (b). The logit is λ\lambda-Lipschitz in each argument with λ=2​d​‖WQ‖​‖WK‖/(r​dh)\lambda=2d\,\|W_{Q}\|\|W_{K}\|/(r\sqrt{d_{h}}), again by (b). The MLP update is μ\mu-Lipschitz with μ=Lip⁡(σ)​‖W2‖​‖W1‖​ 2​d/r\mu=\mathrm{Lip}(\sigma)\|W_{2}\|\|W_{1}\|\,2\sqrt{d}/r. The constants are summed over heads in Appendix A. ∎

Lemma 2 (Dilution).

Let ai​ja_{ij} denote the attention weights of a head. For every query ii and every set JJ of keys, ∑j∈Jai​j≤|J|​e2​B/ni\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}\leq|J|\,e^{2B}/n_{i}, where nin_{i} is the number of keys visible to the query. In particular, a continuation query at distance ii pays at most P​e2​B/(P+i)≤P​e2​B/iPe^{2B}/(P+i)\leq Pe^{2B}/i to the prompt, in either run.

Proof.

By definition, ai​j=esi​j/∑kesi​k≤esi​j−mink⁡si​k/ni≤e2​B/nia_{ij}=e^{s_{ij}}/\sum_{k}e^{s_{ik}}\leq e^{s_{ij}-\min_{k}s_{ik}}/n_{i}\leq e^{2B}/n_{i} and a prompt of length P′≤PP^{\prime}\leq P gives P′/(P′+i)≤P/(P+i)P^{\prime}/(P^{\prime}+i)\leq P/(P+i). ∎

Lemma 3 (One-layer recursion).

Throughout, V,ρ,λ​VV,\rho,\lambda V are the multi-head constants of Appendix A, already summed over heads. For i≥1i\geq 1,

δl​(i)≤K1​δl−1​(i)+K2i​∑j=1iδl−1​(j)+K3​Pi,\delta_{l}(i)\;\leq\;K_{1}\,\delta_{l-1}(i)\;+\;\frac{K_{2}}{i}\sum_{j=1}^{i}\delta_{l-1}(j)\;+\;\frac{K_{3}\,P}{i}, (2)

with K1=(1+μ)​(1+2​λ​V)K_{1}=(1+\mu)(1+2\lambda V), K2=(1+μ)​e2​B​(ρ+2​λ​V)K_{2}=(1+\mu)\,e^{2B}(\rho+2\lambda V) and K3=3​(1+μ)​e2​B​VK_{3}=3(1+\mu)\,e^{2B}V for a sequential block; for a parallel block the same bound holds with K1=(1+μ)+2​λ​VK_{1}=(1+\mu)+2\lambda V, which is no larger.

Proof.

We give the main steps; the full proof, with the constants per head and the alignment of positions, is in Appendix A. Fix a head and a continuation query ii, and let uju_{j}, uj′u^{\prime}_{j} be the value-output vectors of the two runs. The prompts may have different lengths, so we separate the prompt from the continuation, whose ii keys are the same in both runs and sit at the same relative positions. Let π=∑j∈promptai​j\pi=\sum_{j\in\text{prompt}}a_{ij} and a^i​j=ai​j/(1−π)\hat{a}_{ij}=a_{ij}/(1-\pi) for the continuation keys j≤ij\leq i, and write the head output as a=π​a¯P+(1−π)​a¯Ca=\pi\bar{a}_{\mathrm{P}}+(1-\pi)\bar{a}_{\mathrm{C}}, with a¯P=π−1​∑j∈promptai​j​uj\bar{a}_{\mathrm{P}}=\pi^{-1}\sum_{j\in\text{prompt}}a_{ij}u_{j} and a¯C=∑j≤ia^i​j​uj\bar{a}_{\mathrm{C}}=\sum_{j\leq i}\hat{a}_{ij}u_{j}; both have norm at most VV, and similarly for the primed run. Then

a−a′=(1−π)​(a¯C−a¯C′)+(π′−π)​a¯C′+π​a¯P−π′​a¯P′.a-a^{\prime}=(1-\pi)(\bar{a}_{\mathrm{C}}-\bar{a}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{C}})+(\pi^{\prime}-\pi)\,\bar{a}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{C}}+\pi\,\bar{a}_{\mathrm{P}}-\pi^{\prime}\,\bar{a}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{P}}.

Prompt terms.

By Lemma 2, π,π′≤P​e2​B/i\pi,\pi^{\prime}\leq Pe^{2B}/i, hence also |π−π′|≤P​e2​B/i|\pi-\pi^{\prime}|\leq Pe^{2B}/i, and the last three terms are at most 3​V​P​e2​B/i3V\,Pe^{2B}/i.

Continuation term.

The weights a^i​j\hat{a}_{ij} are a softmax over the same ii keys in both runs, with logits in [−B,B][-B,B], so by Lemma 4 in Appendix A we have a^i​j≤e2​B/i\hat{a}_{ij}\leq e^{2B}/i, also along the linear interpolation between the logits of the two runs. Write

a¯C−a¯C′=∑ja^i​j​(uj−uj′)⏟(i)+∑j(a^i​j−a^i​j′)​uj′⏟(ii).\bar{a}_{\mathrm{C}}-\bar{a}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{C}}=\underbrace{\sum_{j}\hat{a}_{ij}(u_{j}-u^{\prime}_{j})}_{(\mathrm{i})}+\underbrace{\sum_{j}(\hat{a}_{ij}-\hat{a}^{\prime}_{ij})u^{\prime}_{j}}_{(\mathrm{ii})}.

The first sum (i) is at most ρ​∑ja^i​j​δl−1​(j)≤ρ​e2​B​i−1​∑j≤iδl−1​(j)\rho\sum_{j}\hat{a}_{ij}\delta_{l-1}(j)\leq\rho e^{2B}i^{-1}\sum_{j\leq i}\delta_{l-1}(j).

For the second sum (ii), the derivative of softmax gives ‖a^i−a^i′‖1≤2​suppath∑ja^i​j​|si​j−si​j′|\|\hat{a}_{i}-\hat{a}^{\prime}_{i}\|_{1}\leq 2\sup_{\text{path}}\sum_{j}\hat{a}_{ij}|s_{ij}-s^{\prime}_{ij}| (Lemma 4 in Appendix A), and |si​j−si​j′|≤λ⁡(δl−1​(i)+δl−1​(j))|s_{ij}-s^{\prime}_{ij}|\leq\lambda(\delta_{l-1}(i)+\delta_{l-1}(j)), so (ii) is at most 2​λ​V​(δl−1​(i)+e2​B​i−1​∑j≤iδl−1​(j))2\lambda V\big(\delta_{l-1}(i)+e^{2B}i^{-1}\sum_{j\leq i}\delta_{l-1}(j)\big).

Since 1−π≤11-\pi\leq 1, summing over heads (absorbed in the constants V,ρ,λ​VV,\rho,\lambda V) gives

‖a−a′‖≤2​λ​V​δl−1​(i)+e2​B​(ρ+2​λ​V)​i−1​∑j≤iδl−1​(j)+3​V​e2​B​P/i.\|a-a^{\prime}\|\leq 2\lambda V\delta_{l-1}(i)+e^{2B}(\rho+2\lambda V)\,i^{-1}\sum_{j\leq i}\delta_{l-1}(j)+3Ve^{2B}P/i.

Residual and MLP.

The residual adds δl−1​(i)\delta_{l-1}(i). In a sequential block the MLP reads the post-attention residual, whose difference is at most δl−1​(i)+‖a−a′‖\delta_{l-1}(i)+\|a-a^{\prime}\|, and multiplies it by at most 1+μ1+\mu, so δl​(i)≤(1+μ)​(δl−1​(i)+‖a−a′‖)\delta_{l}(i)\leq(1+\mu)\big(\delta_{l-1}(i)+\|a-a^{\prime}\|\big). In a parallel block the MLP reads hl−1h_{l-1} and the resulting bound δl​(i)≤(1+μ)​δl−1​(i)+‖a−a′‖\delta_{l}(i)\leq(1+\mu)\delta_{l-1}(i)+\|a-a^{\prime}\| is smaller. Collecting terms gives (2) with the constants stated, for the sequential case; the parallel case follows from the smaller δl​(i)\delta_{l}(i) above. ∎

In words, (2) says that the offset at layer ll and position ii is bounded by three contributions: the offset at the same position one layer earlier, the average offset over all earlier positions (the relay term), and the prompt’s direct contribution, which is O⁡(P/i)O(P/i). Only the last term shrinks with ii; the relay term is what carries prompt information through depth.

4.3 The conditional no-hair theorem

Now we give the following theorem where the no-hair analogy becomes precise.

Theorem 1 (Conditional no-hair theorem).

Under Assumption 1, for every t≥1t\geq 1,

δL​(t)≤CL​P​(L+ln⁡t)L−1t,CL≤K3​∑m=0L−1(K1+2​K2)m,\delta_{L}(t)\;\leq\;C_{L}\,\frac{P\,\big(L+\ln t\big)^{L-1}}{t},\qquad C_{L}\;\leq\;K_{3}\sum_{m=0}^{L-1}(K_{1}+2K_{2})^{m}, (3)

where we recall that δL​(t)\delta_{L}(t) is the norm of the prompt offset at the final layer after tt generated tokens, that PP bounds the length of the two prompts, and that LL is the depth. The theorem bounds this offset by a constant CLC_{L} that depends on the architecture but not on tt or PP, and a decay in tt that is at worst t−1t^{-1} up to logarithmic factors.

Proof.

We prove by induction on ll that δl​(i)≤Al​P​ℓ​(i)l−1/i\delta_{l}(i)\leq A_{l}P\,\ell(i)^{l-1}/i, with ℓ⁡(i)=L+ln⁡i≥1\ell(i)=L+\ln i\geq 1.

For l=1l=1, δ0≡0\delta_{0}\equiv 0, and (2) gives A1=K3A_{1}=K_{3}.

For 2≤l≤L2\leq l\leq L, put k=l−2k=l-2. The function f⁡(s)=ℓ​(s)k/sf(s)=\ell(s)^{k}/s is decreasing on [1,∞)[1,\infty), since f′​(s)=ℓ​(s)k−1​(k−ℓ⁡(s))/s2f^{\prime}(s)=\ell(s)^{k-1}\big(k-\ell(s)\big)/s^{2} and ℓ⁡(s)≥L>k\ell(s)\geq L>k. Hence

∑j≤if⁡(j)≤f⁡(1)+∫1if⁡(s)​𝑑s≤Lk+ℓ​(i)k+1k+1≤(1L+1k+1)​ℓ​(i)k+1≤ 2​ℓ​(i)l−1.\sum_{j\leq i}f(j)\;\leq\;f(1)+\int_{1}^{i}f(s)\,ds\;\leq\;L^{k}+\frac{\ell(i)^{k+1}}{k+1}\;\leq\;\Big(\tfrac{1}{L}+\tfrac{1}{k+1}\Big)\ell(i)^{k+1}\;\leq\;2\,\ell(i)^{l-1}.

With ℓ​(i)l−2≤ℓ​(i)l−1\ell(i)^{l-2}\leq\ell(i)^{l-1} and 1≤ℓ​(i)l−11\leq\ell(i)^{l-1} for the other two terms, (2) yields

Al≤(K1+2​K2)​Al−1+K3.A_{l}\;\leq\;(K_{1}+2K_{2})\,A_{l-1}+K_{3}.

Unrolling gives CL=AL≤K3​∑m=0L−1(K1+2​K2)mC_{L}=A_{L}\leq K_{3}\sum_{m=0}^{L-1}(K_{1}+2K_{2})^{m}. Since K1=(1+μ)​(1+2​λ​V)≥1K_{1}=(1+\mu)(1+2\lambda V)\geq 1, each term in the sum is at least 11, so the sum is at most L​(K1+2​K2)L−1L\,(K_{1}+2K_{2})^{L-1} and CL≤L​K3​(K1+2​K2)L−1C_{L}\leq L\,K_{3}\,(K_{1}+2K_{2})^{L-1}. Since (L+ln⁡t)L−1∼(ln⁡t)L−1(L+\ln t)^{L-1}\sim(\ln t)^{L-1}, the asymptotic form is O⁡(P​(ln⁡t)L−1/t)O\big(P(\ln t)^{L-1}/t\big). ∎

Remark 1 (What the constant does and does not control).

The constant is large and grows with depth. CLC_{L} can grow exponentially with depth, and the bound is stated in terms of e2​Be^{2B}, which is large. Lemma 2 only uses the spread Δ=maxk⁡si​k−mink⁡si​k\Delta=\max_{k}s_{ik}-\min_{k}s_{ik} of the logits seen by each query, so e2​Be^{2B} can be replaced by eΔe^{\Delta}; but in trained networks with attention sinks Δ\Delta is large, and the gain is limited.

What Theorem 1 fixes is the asymptotic shape, not a numerical prediction. The bound is informative only once t≫P​eΔt\gg Pe^{\Delta}, which for trained networks lies beyond any window we measure. What it fixes is that no decay is slower than t−1t^{-1} up to at most L−1L-1 powers of ln⁡t\ln t, one per relay round; the shift LL inside the logarithm only matters for small tt. It does not predict the exponents fitted over finite windows. Those are compared with the exactly solvable model of Proposition 2, not with (3).

How large Δ\Delta can be is observed in practice. For Pythia-160m we measure, over late queries of 400 prompt–continuation pairs, the spread of each query’s logits, ln⁡(maxk⁡αi​k/mink⁡αi​k)\ln(\max_{k}\alpha_{ik}/\min_{k}\alpha_{ik}) with αi​k=esi​k\alpha_{ik}=e^{s_{ik}}. At initialisation its median is 1.91.9–2.32.3 (maximum 4.34.3), so eΔe^{\Delta} is of order 10210^{2} and the dilution regime is reached within our windows. After training the median is 1717–1818 in layers 1–3 and saturates the float32 range in the deep layers (≥69\geq 69, the smallest weights underflow): there eΔe^{\Delta} exceeds 10710^{7} and the bound is not informative at any accessible tt.

Remark 2 (From δ\delta to the measured signal).

Since ‖𝔼c​Δ‖≤𝔼c​‖Δ‖\|\mathbb{E}_{c}\Delta\|\leq\mathbb{E}_{c}\|\Delta\|, the signal of Section 3 obeys 𝒮l​(t)≤(𝔼c​δl​(t))2/(d​minj​σl,j2)\mathcal{S}_{l}(t)\leq\big(\mathbb{E}_{c}\,\delta_{l}(t)\big)^{2}/\big(d\,\min_{j}\sigma_{l,j}^{2}\big), so Theorem 1 bounds it as well (averaging over a window only moves tt within the window). The converse fails: offsets whose direction depends on the continuation partly cancel in 𝔼c​Δ\mathbb{E}_{c}\Delta, so 𝒮\mathcal{S} can decay faster than δ2\delta^{2}. We therefore also report the exponent of ℳl\mathcal{M}_{l} (Section 3.3), which is the window-averaged 𝔼c​δl2\mathbb{E}_{c}\delta_{l}^{2} up to the coordinate scaling.

4.4 The exterior carries the hair

Corollary 1 (The exterior carries the hair).

Let p(⋅∣x,c<t)p(\cdot\mid x,c_{<t}) be the next-token distribution given the history c<tc_{<t} (the prefix of the continuation up to time tt), WUW_{U} the unembedding, and εt=‖WU‖2→∞​(2​d/r)​CL​P​(L+ln⁡t)L−1/t\varepsilon_{t}=\|W_{U}\|_{2\to\infty}\,(2\sqrt{d}/r)\,C_{L}\,P\,(L+\ln t)^{L-1}/t, where ‖WU‖2→∞\|W_{U}\|_{2\to\infty} is the operator norm from ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} and TV\mathrm{TV} the total-variation distance. For every history c<tc_{<t},

TV(p(⋅∣x,c<t),p(⋅∣x′,c<t))≤εt=O(P(lnt)L−1/t),\mathrm{TV}\big(p(\cdot\mid x,c_{<t}),\,p(\cdot\mid x^{\prime},c_{<t})\big)\leq\varepsilon_{t}=O\big(P(\ln t)^{L-1}/t\big),

and for every m≥0m\geq 0 the joint laws of the next m+1m+1 tokens given c<tc_{<t} differ in total variation by at most ∑s=tt+mεs≤(m+1)​εt\sum_{s=t}^{t+m}\varepsilon_{s}\leq(m+1)\,\varepsilon_{t}.

Proof.

The final LayerNorm is Lipschitz by Lemma 1(b), and softmax is 11-Lipschitz from ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} logits to total variation; Theorem 1 holds for every continuation, hence for every history. For the joint law, couple the two runs token by token, maximally at each step given a common history: the probability that the coupled sequences first differ at step ss is at most εs\varepsilon_{s}. Finally εs\varepsilon_{s} is non-increasing in ss, by the monotonicity argument in the proof of Theorem 1. ∎

The corollary says what happens over a short window. Over a window short compared with t/(P​(ln⁡t)L−1)t/\big(P(\ln t)^{L-1}\big), the next token is determined, up to (m+1)​εt(m+1)\varepsilon_{t}, by the text generated so far, whichever prompt produced it.

It says nothing about long horizons. The bound applies step by step; the sum ∑sεs\sum_{s}\varepsilon_{s} diverges, so it does not exclude a cumulative influence of the prompt that bypasses the text. Nor does it show that such an influence exists.

Whether the prompt’s influence at late times is in fact carried by the text is therefore an empirical statement, which Section 8 tests, not a consequence of Theorem 1.

This is the sense in which the no-hair theorem holds. In general relativity the quantities that survive are those measurable at infinity, carried by the exterior field; here, step by step, the channel through which a prompt influences what comes next is the exterior record. Section 8 is consistent with this picture: the language of the prompt remains decodable from free generations, but under a shared continuation its imprint in the hidden state still decays, at a rate comparable to that of a one-word change.

4.5 An exactly solvable model

Theorem 1 gives an upper bound, and the bound contains logarithmic powers. Are they an artefact of the proof, or a feature of the architecture? To answer this, we turn to a simplified model that can be solved exactly, which is, the linear relay model. In this model, every head attends uniformly, each block multiplies the offset by a constant gain, and the prompt enters uniformly. The model is solvable in closed form, and its solution has the same P​(ln⁡i)l−1/iP(\ln i)^{l-1}/i shape as the bound, which shows that the logarithmic powers cannot be removed. It also gives a parameter-free prediction for untrained networks, which we compare with the measured curves at the end of this subsection.

The model.

Consider the first-order dynamics of a small offset around a fixed background: every head attends uniformly (ai​j=1/nia_{ij}=1/n_{i}, the regime of a randomly initialised network, whose logits are close to zero), the value-output path of block ll multiplies the offset by a gain gl>0g_{l}>0 along a fixed direction ee, and normalisation and MLPs are replaced by their Jacobians, which we absorb into glg_{l}. The two prompts differ by ee at every prompt position, and we keep this prompt offset fixed through depth (if it grows, every offset below grows, so lower bounds remain valid). The offset at the ii-th continuation token after ll blocks is then δl​(i)​e\delta_{l}(i)\,e with

δl​(i)=δl−1​(i)+glP+i​(P+∑j=1iδl−1​(j)),δ0≡0.\delta_{l}(i)=\delta_{l-1}(i)+\frac{g_{l}}{P+i}\Big(P+\sum_{j=1}^{i}\delta_{l-1}(j)\Big),\qquad\delta_{0}\equiv 0. (4)

The first result says below that the bound from Theorem 1 is attained in this regime: with equal gains, the offset decays with exactly l−1l-1 logarithmic powers, so the exponent cannot be lowered.

Proposition 1 (Uniform attention attains the bound).

In the linear relay model with equal gains gg, for all l,i≥1l,i\geq 1,

gl(l−1)!​P​(ln⁡P+i+1P+1)l−1P+i≤δl​(i)≤Cl​P​(l+ln⁡i)l−1i,Cl≤g​∑m=0l−1(1+2​g)m.\frac{g^{l}}{(l-1)!}\,\frac{P\,\big(\ln\frac{P+i+1}{P+1}\big)^{l-1}}{P+i}\;\leq\;\delta_{l}(i)\;\leq\;C_{l}\,\frac{P\,(l+\ln i)^{l-1}}{i},\qquad C_{l}\leq g\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}(1+2g)^{m}. (5)

Hence δl​(i)=Θ⁡(P​(ln⁡i)l−1/i)\delta_{l}(i)=\Theta\big(P(\ln i)^{l-1}/i\big) as i→∞i\to\infty: the power l−1l-1 in Theorem 1 cannot be lowered.

Proof.

Since P+i≥iP+i\geq i, (4) is of the form (2) with K1=1K_{1}=1 and K2=K3=gK_{2}=K_{3}=g, and the induction in the proof of Theorem 1 applies with LL replaced by ll. The lower bound is the k=lk=l term of the exact solution (6) below, with el=gle_{l}=g^{l} and hl−1≥p1l−1/(l−1)!≥(ln⁡P+i+1P+1)l−1/(l−1)!h_{l-1}\geq p_{1}^{l-1}/(l-1)!\geq\big(\ln\frac{P+i+1}{P+1}\big)^{l-1}/(l-1)!; all other terms are non-negative. ∎

Layer-dependent gains.

The model can also be solved exactly for arbitrary gains, which turns the depth dependence of untrained networks into a prediction.

Proposition 2 (Exact solution with layer gains).

Let xj=1/(P+j)x_{j}=1/(P+j). We write eke_{k} and hkh_{k} for the elementary and the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials in g1,…,glg_{1},\dots,g_{l} and in x1,…,xix_{1},\dots,x_{i} (e0=h0=1e_{0}=h_{0}=1, h−1=0h_{-1}=0). In the linear relay model, for all l,i≥1l,i\geq 1,

δl​(i)=PP+i​∑k=1lek​(g1,…,gl)​hk−1​(x1,…,xi).\delta_{l}(i)\;=\;\frac{P}{P+i}\sum_{k=1}^{l}e_{k}(g_{1},\dots,g_{l})\,h_{k-1}(x_{1},\dots,x_{i}). (6)

Moreover, with u=ln⁡P+iPu=\ln\frac{P+i}{P}, for every k≥1k\geq 1

|hk​(x1,…,xi)−ukk!|≤1P​(uk−1(k−1)!+hk−2​(x1,…,xi)),\Big|h_{k}(x_{1},\dots,x_{i})-\frac{u^{k}}{k!}\Big|\;\leq\;\frac{1}{P}\Big(\frac{u^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}+h_{k-2}(x_{1},\dots,x_{i})\Big), (7)

We first derive (6), then the bound (7).
