Small gains.

When the gains are small, the exact solution reduces to a single-parameter form and gives an explicit expression for the local exponent.

Corollary 2 (Small gains).

Let Gl=∑m≤lgmG_{l}=\sum_{m\leq l}g_{m} and Ql=∑m≤lgm2Q_{l}=\sum_{m\leq l}g_{m}^{2}. Then 0≤Glk/k!−ek≤Ql2​Glk−2/(k−2)!0\leq G_{l}^{k}/k!-e_{k}\leq\frac{Q_{l}}{2}\,G_{l}^{k-2}/(k-2)!. If Ql​u≪GlQ_{l}u\ll G_{l}, Gl≪PG_{l}\ll P and l2≫Gl​ul^{2}\gg G_{l}u (the three error terms of Corollary 3; note that Ql≪Gl2Q_{l}\ll G_{l}^{2} alone does not suffice once Gl​uG_{l}u is large), then

δl​(i)≃PP+i​φ​(Gl,u),φ⁡(G,u)=∑k≥1Gk​uk−1k!​(k−1)!=G/u​I1​(2​G​u),\delta_{l}(i)\simeq\frac{P}{P+i}\,\varphi(G_{l},u),\qquad\varphi(G,u)=\sum_{k\geq 1}\frac{G^{k}u^{k-1}}{k!\,(k-1)!}=\sqrt{G/u}\;I_{1}\big(2\sqrt{Gu}\big), (8)

with I1I_{1} a modified Bessel function, and the local exponent αloc=−dlnδl/dlnt\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}=-d\ln\delta_{l}/d\ln t is

αloc≃tP+t(1−∂ulnφ),∂ulnφ=Gl/u−34​u+O((Glu3)−1/2)(Glu≫1).\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}\simeq\frac{t}{P+t}\big(1-\partial_{u}\ln\varphi\big),\qquad\partial_{u}\ln\varphi=\sqrt{G_{l}/u}-\frac{3}{4u}+O\big((G_{l}u^{3})^{-1/2}\big)\quad(G_{l}u\gg 1). (9)

Depth enters only through the accumulated gain GlG_{l}; Proposition 3 and Corollary 3 in Appendix A bound the error of (8) explicitly. Moreover (a) αloc→1\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}\to 1 as t→∞t\to\infty, and (b) at fixed tt, αloc\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}} does not increase as GlG_{l} grows, hence decreases with depth. Over a finite window the measured exponent of an untrained network is therefore below 11, lower in deeper layers, and creeps up as the window is extended.

Proof.

For the bound on eke_{k}, write Gk/k!=∑mgm/m!G^{k}/k!=\sum_{m}g^{m}/m! over multisets of size kk and eke_{k} as the sum over those without repeated index; a multiset with a repeated index rr contributes at most gr22\tfrac{g_{r}^{2}}{2} times a term of Gk−2/(k−2)!G^{k-2}/(k-2)!. Inserting ek≃Gk/k!e_{k}\simeq G^{k}/k! and hk−1≃uk−1/(k−1)!h_{k-1}\simeq u^{k-1}/(k-1)! (Proposition 2) into (6) gives (8); the terms of the series peak at k≈G​uk\approx\sqrt{Gu}, so the truncation at k=lk=l is immaterial. Since d​u/d​ln⁡t=t/(P+t)du/d\ln t=t/(P+t), αloc=tP+t​(1−∂uln⁡φ)\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}=\frac{t}{P+t}(1-\partial_{u}\ln\varphi), and the expansion follows from I1(z)=ez(2πz)−1/2(1+O(1/z))I_{1}(z)=e^{z}(2\pi z)^{-1/2}(1+O(1/z)). For (a), ∂uln⁡φ→0\partial_{u}\ln\varphi\to 0. For (b), write φ=G​F​(G​u)\varphi=G\,F(Gu) with F⁡(z)=∑kzk−1/(k!​(k−1)!)F(z)=\sum_{k}z^{k-1}/(k!(k-1)!), so ∂uln⁡φ=u−1​ζ​(G​u)\partial_{u}\ln\varphi=u^{-1}\zeta(Gu) with ζ⁡(z)=z​F′​(z)/F⁡(z)\zeta(z)=zF^{\prime}(z)/F(z). Now ζ⁡(z)\zeta(z) is the mean of k−1k-1 under weights proportional to zk−1/(k!​(k−1)!)z^{k-1}/(k!(k-1)!), and its derivative in ln⁡z\ln z is the corresponding variance, so ζ\zeta is non-decreasing and ∂uln⁡φ\partial_{u}\ln\varphi is non-decreasing in GG. ∎

Comparison with experiment.

The model makes two parameter-free predictions for the first blocks. In layer 1, δ1=g1​P/(P+i)\delta_{1}=g_{1}P/(P+i), so the local exponent is exactly t/(P+t)t/(P+t). In layer 2, φ2=(g1+g2)+g1​g2​h1\varphi_{2}=(g_{1}+g_{2})+g_{1}g_{2}h_{1}, so (1−P+tt​αloc)−1=h1+g1+g2g1​g2\big(1-\tfrac{P+t}{t}\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}\big)^{-1}=h_{1}+\tfrac{g_{1}+g_{2}}{g_{1}g_{2}} is linear in h1≈uh_{1}\approx u with slope exactly 11, whatever the gains. Untrained Pythia is consistent with both (Section 5: the layer-1 law with PeffP_{\mathrm{eff}} close to the prompt length, fitted power 1.071.07–1.331.33 in layer 2); untrained Qwen is consistent with neither, so its first blocks are not in the linear-relay regime. In deeper layers the effective power seen over a finite window depends on the gains, not only on the layer index, so the coincidence k≈l−1k\approx l-1 in layers 2–4 of Pythia should not be read as a general law.

Small-gain fit. Fitting (9) without the factor t/(P+t)t/(P+t) and the 3/(4​u)3/(4u) term to untrained Pythia-1b on real-corpus pairs (P≈28P\approx 28, unbiased signal, centre-labelled windows) gives R2≥0.99R^{2}\geq 0.99 in layers 3–15, with Gl=0.36,0.52,0.95,1.20,1.35G_{l}=0.36,0.52,0.95,1.20,1.35 in layers 3,4,8,12,153,4,8,12,15 and increments of roughly 0.65/l0.65/l per layer, i.e. Gl≈0.65​ln⁡l+constG_{l}\approx 0.65\ln l+\mathrm{const}. Repeating the fit in all fifteen layers gives Gl=0.60​ln⁡l−0.29G_{l}=0.60\ln l-0.29 (R2=0.997R^{2}=0.997, largest residual 0.050.05) and per-layer increments gl∝l−0.94g_{l}\propto l^{-0.94}; the fitted logarithmic power follows k=2.09​ln⁡l−0.12k=2.09\ln l-0.12 (R2=0.9998R^{2}=0.9998). Over our windows, however, Gl​u≤5G_{l}u\leq 5 (and ≤1.3\leq 1.3 in layer 3), outside the range of (9), so these values are effective parameters rather than estimates of the accumulated gain.

Exact-solution fit. The exact solution (6) turns them into estimates. We fit it to the same curves layer by layer, with the exact recursion and one free amplitude per layer (the coordinate normalisation of 𝒮\mathcal{S} is layer dependent), so that each layer is fitted on the shape of its curve only. Layer 1 fixes PP whatever the gains; it gives P=28.8P=28.8, against a mean prompt length of 25.725.7 tokens, with R2=0.9999R^{2}=0.9999 and a largest deviation of the local exponent of 0.0260.026. Since δl\delta_{l} depends on the gains only through the symmetric functions ek​(g1,…,gl)e_{k}(g_{1},\dots,g_{l}), layer 2 constrains only g1​g2/(g1+g2)g_{1}g_{2}/(g_{1}+g_{2}); we fit g1,g2,g3g_{1},g_{2},g_{3} jointly on layers 2–3 and then, from layer 4 on, one new gain per layer with the earlier ones fixed, so that a single parameter predicts the whole curve of each layer. All fifteen curves are reproduced with R2≥0.992R^{2}\geq 0.992; the largest deviation between measured and predicted local exponents grows from 0.050.05 in layer 2 to 0.080.08 in layer 15, so the one-gain-per-layer model captures the curves well but not perfectly in the deep layers.

Identifying the first two gains. Layer 2 alone constrains g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} only through g1​g2/(g1+g2)g_{1}g_{2}/(g_{1}+g_{2}); together with layer 3 they are determined as an unordered pair, since every δl\delta_{l} is symmetric in g1,…,glg_{1},\dots,g_{l}, so g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} cannot be told apart. The fit returns equal values, g^1=g^2=0.66\hat{g}_{1}=\hat{g}_{2}=0.66.

A test of the symmetry. This is not an artefact of the starting point: restarting the joint fit of g1,g2,g3g_{1},g_{2},g_{3} from six widely different initial values, including strongly asymmetric ones (e.g. (0.05,2,0.2)(0.05,2,0.2) and (2,0.2,0.5)(2,0.2,0.5)), reaches the same minimum (g^1,g^2,g^3)=(0.664,0.664,0.24)(\hat{g}_{1},\hat{g}_{2},\hat{g}_{3})=(0.664,0.664,0.24) at the same cost each time, and on synthetic curves generated with an unequal pair (0.65,0.325)(0.65,0.325) the same fit, started on the symmetric diagonal, leaves it and recovers the unequal values, so the equality is a property of the data and not of the optimiser.

The remaining gains. The gains then decrease as g^l∝l−1.4\hat{g}_{l}\propto l^{-1.4} (layers 4–15), to 0.020.02 in layer 15, with G^15=2.18\hat{G}_{15}=2.18; a joint fit of all gains gives the same values to within 0.090.09. The first gains are not small, which is why the effective GlG_{l} of the small-gain fit differ from these estimates.

Remark 3 (Physics analogy).

Lemma 2 is a Gauss-law statement: a fixed charge spread over a growing volume. Relay plays the role of back-scattering off the background curvature, which in general relativity produces late-time power-law tails (Price, 1972). Trained networks scatter little; untrained ones scatter a lot. We use the analogy as a guide only.

5 Forgetting is close to a power law

We now turn to the measurement. The theory of Section 4 predicts the shape of the decay but not its rate; the rate is the exponent αl\alpha_{l} defined in Section 3, and this section reports the corresponding results.

5.1 Hand-written scenes

Table 1 gives the exponent α\alpha for Pythia-160m and 410m at initialisation and after training. Five patterns are visible, and they carry over to the real-corpus pairs of Section 5.2.

  • •

    Noise does not decay. β≈0\beta\approx 0 for every Pythia model, layer and checkpoint (untrained Qwen is the exception, Section 5.4), so all the change in decodability comes from α\alpha. Since 𝒩\mathcal{N} is the spread of hidden states across continuations, this is what stationarity of the continuation text implies; we report it as a check rather than as a finding.

  • •

    Layer 1 is pure dilution. After the first attention block the continuation tokens are still identical in the two runs, so no relay is possible and only the direct path exists. In untrained models the local exponent follows the dilution law of a uniform head, ln⁡P+t2P+t1/ln⁡t2t1\ln\frac{P+t_{2}}{P+t_{1}}\big/\ln\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}} between consecutive points, with a single fitted PeffP_{\mathrm{eff}} to within 0.030.03 at every octave; the fitted value tracks the prompt length (Peff≈17P_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 17 for the hand-written scenes, ≈30\approx 30 for the longer real-corpus prompts). Trained models give α≈1\alpha\approx 1 in layer 1 (1.051.05 and 1.011.01 here, 0.940.94–0.970.97 on real-corpus pairs).

  • •

    Relay enters after layer 2 in trained models. Layers 1–2 stay at 0.90.9–1.051.05; deeper layers settle at 0.570.57–0.700.70 (both sizes) and are roughly flat with depth.

  • •

    At initialisation, α\alpha depends on the layer index, not on width. At matched layers the two untrained models agree exactly (L1 0.820.82/0.820.82, L2 0.650.65/0.650.65, L6 0.470.47/0.470.47). In layer 1 this is automatic: pure dilution depends only on the prompt length, which is the same for both models (same tokenizer). The agreement in deeper layers is informative: in the linear relay model (Proposition 2) it means that the gains at a given layer index do not depend on the width. This is not because the initial weights match. The released step-0 checkpoints follow small_init for the input projections (standard deviation 2/5​d\sqrt{2/5d}: 0.02280.0228, 0.01980.0198, 0.01400.0140 for 160m, 410m, 1b) and wang_init for the output projections (2/(L​d)2/(L\sqrt{d}): 0.00600.0060, 0.00260.0026, 0.00280.0028), so the absolute size of each block’s write differs between the three models and depends on their total depth. A scale-free mechanism is needed. A natural candidate is that what matters is the write of a block relative to the residual stream it adds to, which at initialisation is itself made of the earlier writes: the pre-norm activations grow as l\sqrt{l} with depth (Pythia-160m: ‖Π​h‖/d≈0.12​l\|\Pi h\|/\sqrt{d}\approx 0.12\sqrt{l} to within 0.010.01 from block 1 to block 11), so the relative write of block ll, and with it the gain, depends on ll but not on the absolute scale.

  • •

    Content-agnostic vs. content-dependent. At initialisation the axes have the same α\alpha to within 0.040.04; after training they separate, in the same order for both sizes (deep layers on hand-written scenes: paraphrase 0.500.50–0.570.57, detail 0.650.65–0.750.75).

Local exponents rise towards 11.

If δl​(t)∝(ln⁡t)k/t\delta_{l}(t)\propto(\ln t)^{k}/t, the local exponent is αloc=1−k/ln⁡(t/t0)\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}=1-k/\ln(t/t_{0}) for some reference time t0t_{0}. Then 1/(1−αloc)1/(1-\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}) is linear in ln⁡t\ln t with slope 1/k1/k, and we use kk as a descriptive effective power. For untrained networks αloc\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}} rises monotonically with tt in every layer, as Corollary 2 predicts: in Pythia-160m, from 0.470.47 to 0.990.99 in layer 1, and from 0.210.21 to 0.530.53 in layer 11. The linear form fits with R2≥0.985R^{2}\geq 0.985 (Table 2). In layer 2 the fitted power is close to 11 (1.071.07–1.081.08), the value the linear relay model gives for any gains (Section 4.5, Comparison with experiment). In layer 3 it is close to 22 (1.961.96), and from layer 6 on it grows much more slowly than l−1l-1 (k/ln⁡l≈2.0k/\ln l\approx 2.0–2.22.2 in both models), as expected when the gains are small. These fits ignore the factor t/(P+t)t/(P+t) of (9); the exact solution (6) is the appropriate model for the full curves. The small-gain form of Corollary 2 fits the same local exponents at least as well, and we compare the two on the real-corpus pairs, where the unbiased signal is available.

5.2 Real-corpus prompt pairs

To rule out an artefact of hand-written scenes we repeat the measurement on 100 pairs per axis drawn from real corpora: a WikiText-103 test sentence vs. the same sentence with one content word swapped (detail); MRPC paraphrase pairs (para); WMT14 English sentences vs. their French translations (lang); and two random WikiText sentences (unrelated), the largest possible difference. Continuations are WikiText-103 validation chunks, te∈[16,1024]t_{e}\in[16,1024], 8 continuations per pair, unbiased signal; intervals are over prompt pairs (Table 3).

Every finding carries over. At initialisation α\alpha falls with depth and the local exponent rises monotonically with tt in every layer; the fitted powers are k=1.33,2.11k=1.33,2.11 in layers 2 and 3 (R2≥0.97R^{2}\geq 0.97), then k/ln⁡l≈2.0k/\ln l\approx 2.0; the layer-1 local exponent follows the dilution law with Peff≈30P_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 30, close to the length of these prompts (26–32 tokens on average), against ≈17\approx 17 for the shorter hand-written ones: the prompt’s share of the context scales with its length. After training, layers 1–2 stay at 0.80.8–11 and deeper layers at 0.520.52–0.700.70, with paraphrase and language forgotten most slowly.

Two descriptions of the untrained curves.

Corollary 2 predicts that (1−αloc)−2(1-\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}})^{-2} is linear in ln⁡P+tP\ln\frac{P+t}{P} with slope 1/Gl1/G_{l}. On the real-corpus pairs this holds with R2≥0.99R^{2}\geq 0.99 from layer 3 on (Pythia-160m: Gl=0.35,0.74,0.99,1.13G_{l}=0.35,0.74,0.99,1.13 in layers 3,6,9,113,6,9,11, R2≥0.992R^{2}\geq 0.992; Pythia-1b in Table 2), at least as well as the pure logarithmic form. In Pythia-1b the increments of GlG_{l} per layer are about 0.65/l0.65/l, i.e. Gl≈0.65​ln⁡l+constG_{l}\approx 0.65\ln l+\mathrm{const}, as expected if the gain of a layer shrinks as the residual stream it writes into grows; these are effective parameters rather than estimates of the accumulated gain. Over our windows the two descriptions cannot be told apart.

Scale: Pythia-1b.

Table 4 repeats the real-corpus measurement on Pythia-1b (16 layers, width 2048) with the same 100 pairs per axis. At initialisation the exponents coincide with those of Pythia-160m at matched layers to two decimals (L1–L3: 0.73,0.57,0.500.73,0.57,0.50 for both), the local exponent rises monotonically in every layer, and the fitted logarithmic powers are k=1.33,2.14,2.78k=1.33,2.14,2.78 in layers 2, 3, 4, close to l−1l-1 (R2≥0.97R^{2}\geq 0.97), with k/ln⁡l≈2.0k/\ln l\approx 2.0–2.12.1 beyond. After training, layer 1 is at 0.870.87, layer 2 at 0.790.79, and deep layers settle at 0.580.58–0.610.61; paraphrase is again forgotten most slowly (0.520.52 in the last layer) and the unrelated axis again matches the one-word detail axis. Across a 6×6\times increase in parameters we see no qualitative change.

A second model family: Qwen2.5.

Qwen2.5 differs from Pythia in its normalisation (RMSNorm), its residual structure (sequential) and its attention (grouped-query); we measure it on the real-corpus pairs with te∈[16,2048]t_{e}\in[16,2048] (Table 4). Trained Qwen2.5-0.5B gives 0.740.74 in layer 1, 0.690.69 in layers 2–3 and 0.540.54–0.620.62 beyond; Qwen2.5-1.5B gives 0.950.95 in layer 1, 0.810.81 in layer 2 and 0.550.55–0.630.63 beyond, the same profile as the trained Pythia models. At random initialisation α\alpha falls from 0.630.63 (layer 1) to 0.180.18 (layer 23), and the local exponent rises monotonically with tt in every layer. In the untrained model a one-character change of the prompt remains linearly decodable after 512 tokens; in the trained model it does not. Section 5.4 discusses where Qwen departs from the linear relay picture.

The unrelated axis gives the sharpest test of the geometric picture: two completely different sentences are forgotten at the same rate as a one-word substitution (Pythia-160m, layer 11: 0.350.35 vs. 0.370.37 at initialisation, 0.700.70 vs. 0.690.69 after training). The size of the difference sets the amplitude of the offset, not its decay exponent.

5.3 Signal versus mean squared offset

In untrained Pythia the exponents of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and of the mean squared offset ℳ\mathcal{M} coincide to within 0.010.01 in every layer: the offset points in the same direction whatever the continuation. After training ℳ\mathcal{M} decays more slowly in the deep layers (Pythia-160m: αℳ=0.52\alpha_{\mathcal{M}}=0.52–0.570.57 against α𝒮=0.58\alpha_{\mathcal{S}}=0.58–0.670.67 in layers 6–11; Qwen2.5-0.5B: 0.520.52–0.580.58 against 0.550.55–0.620.62), and in untrained Qwen much more slowly (0.100.10–0.210.21 against 0.180.18–0.260.26 in layers 6–23). Part of the decay of 𝒮\mathcal{S} in these models is therefore the decorrelation of the offset’s direction across continuations, as anticipated in Remark 2; the norm of the offset itself decays more slowly.

5.4 Where Qwen differs

Two features of the untrained Qwen model do not carry over from Pythia. First, the layer-1 local exponent does not follow the dilution law with a single PeffP_{\mathrm{eff}} (residuals up to 0.130.13), and the fitted powers are k=2.9,4.5k=2.9,4.5 in layers 2, 3 (k/ln⁡l≈4k/\ln l\approx 4–55 beyond; Gl=0.56G_{l}=0.56–4.94.9). The linear relay model gives exactly the dilution law in layer 1 and a power of exactly 11 in layer 2 for any gains (Section 4.5), so the first blocks of untrained Qwen are not in the linear-relay regime, although the qualitative predictions (local exponent rising towards 11, decreasing with depth) hold. This is not in conflict with Theorem 1, which bounds δ\delta asymptotically and says nothing about its local slope at finite tt. Attention in untrained Qwen is as uniform as in untrained Pythia (normalised entropy 0.9900.990–0.9930.993, largest weight 0.0060.006–0.0070.007 in layers 1–3, logit spread median ≈2\approx 2), so non-uniform attention is not the reason. A difference that is present is the block structure: Pythia uses parallel residual connections, so its first MLP sees only the embedding, which is the same in both runs, and the layer-1 offset is exactly the attention write; Qwen’s blocks are sequential, so the MLP of the first block already processes the attention write nonlinearly, and at initialisation that write dominates the residual (mid-block norm 0.0330.033, against about 0.020.02 for embeddings drawn with standard deviation 0.020.02). We take this as the likely reason the linear relay model fails in the first blocks of Qwen, without having tested it. Second, the noise across continuations grows slowly at initialisation (β≈−0.1\beta\approx-0.1 to −0.2-0.2 in layers 2–23), so the decodability of the prompt decays as t−2​(α−β)t^{-2(\alpha-\beta)} rather than t−2​αt^{-2\alpha}.

A late slowdown in trained Qwen.

With windows up to 20482048, the local exponent of the trained Qwen models decreases at late times. In Qwen2.5-0.5B this happens in every layer, down to 0.230.23–0.570.57 in the last octave, including layer 1 (0.240.24), where only the direct path exists. In Qwen2.5-1.5B layers 1–2 keep decaying fast (last octave 2.22.2 and 1.31.3) while layers 3–27 slow down to 0.380.38–0.530.53. In layers 14 and 21 of Qwen2.5-1.5B the signal stays below three times its sampling floor at all windows, so those two layers are not interpreted.

Three explanations excluded. We first excluded a statistical explanation: with nc=8n_{c}=8 continuations the plug-in signal is biased upwards by Varc⁡Δ/nc\operatorname{Var}_{c}\Delta/n_{c}, which would flatten the curve late; with the unbiased estimator the slowdown is unchanged (Qwen2.5-0.5B, last octave: 0.24,0.42,0.430.24,0.42,0.43 in layers 1–3). We then tested a prompt-specific attention sink: Lemma 2 bounds the attention to the prompt by P​e2​B/iPe^{2B}/i, which only bites once i≫e2​Bi\gg e^{2B}, and without a BOS token the sink is the first prompt token, which differs between the two prompts of most pairs. Prepending the same token (<|endoftext|>) to both prompts, which makes the sink shared, leaves the slowdown unchanged (last octave 0.24,0.40,0.440.24,0.40,0.44 in layers 1–3). Finally we tested the structure of the continuation text: WikiText chunks span headings and document boundaries, which affect all prompts alike and are only probed at the largest windows. Replacing the continuations by WikiText sentences in random order, which removes headings, document boundaries and any structure beyond a sentence, leaves the slowdown unchanged as well (last octave 0.23,0.49,0.470.23,0.49,0.47 in layers 1–3 and 0.180.18–0.570.57 in the deep layers, against 0.24,0.42,0.430.24,0.42,0.43 and 0.230.23–0.570.57); the global exponents move by at most 0.060.06 (slightly lower in the deep layers). Three explanations are thus excluded: estimation bias, a prompt-specific sink, and the long-range structure of the continuation.

A positional oscillation. Since the slowdown appears in layer 1, where only the direct path exists, what remains is the dependence of attention on distance. We measured it directly: in the first block of trained Qwen2.5-0.5B, the attention that continuation queries pay to the prompt follows 1/t1/t on average out to t=2048t=2048, with (P+t)(P+t) times the attention mass between 66 and 1111 from t=64t=64 on, but it oscillates by about ±30%\pm 30\% around that law from octave to octave (log-slopes −0.94,−0.42,−1.25,−1.38,−0.64-0.94,-0.42,-1.25,-1.38,-0.64 between consecutive windows from t=64t=64). The local exponents of the layer-1 offset follow these oscillations: the steep octave 512512–10241024 (attention slope −1.38-1.38) is where αloc\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}} exceeds 11, and the shallower last octave (−0.64-0.64) is where it drops to 0.240.24. The late slowdown in layer 1 is therefore an oscillation of the direct path around dilution, of positional origin, rather than a breakdown of dilution; its amplitude in the offset is larger than in the attention mass, so the value vectors contribute as well. In block 2, (P+t)(P+t) times the attention mass rises slowly with tt (1212 to 1717 between t=128t=128 and 20482048), a mild departure from 1/t1/t at long range. The slowdown is absent from layers 1–2 of Qwen2.5-1.5B, whose attention we have not measured; tying the period of the oscillation to the rotary frequencies is left open.

5.5 Continuation structure

For trained networks on contiguous WikiText, αloc\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}} shows no systematic trend over 1616–19201920 in the deep layers of Pythia (a power law over two decades), with a recurring bump at 128128–256256 in both sizes. Repeating the measurement with shuffled-sentence continuations, which keep the vocabulary and the sentences of WikiText but remove all structure beyond a sentence, separates three effects (Table 5).

  • •

    Untrained networks do not notice. For untrained Pythia-160m every exponent, every local exponent and every fitted kk and GlG_{l} agrees with the contiguous-text values to within 0.010.01: geometric dilution and relay at initialisation are independent of what the text says, as the theory requires.

  • •

    The first layers do not notice either. In trained models layers 1–4, where the direct path dominates, change by at most 0.040.04. The bump of the layer-1 local exponent at 128128–256256 in Pythia-160m survives (1.621.62 against 1.541.54), so it is positional, not a property of the text.

  • •

    Deep layers of trained models forget more slowly on unstructured text. The global exponents drop by 0.020.02–0.110.11 in layers 6–11 of Pythia-160m and by 0.090.09–0.180.18 in layers 8–15 of Pythia-1b (by ≤0.06\leq 0.06 in Qwen2.5-0.5B). The shape of the local exponent changes in a model-dependent way: it rises from about 0.450.45 to about 1.01.0 across the window in Pythia-160m, and falls from about 0.50.5 to about 0.30.3 in Pythia-1b.

The pure power law of the trained deep layers is therefore a property of the model on coherent text. A natural reading is that a coherent continuation gives the deep layers relevant recent content to attend to, which displaces the prompt; without that structure the prompt competes for longer. We have not tested this mechanism. The ordering of the axes and the trained–untrained contrast are unaffected. In layers 1–2 of the trained models the local exponents fluctuate above 11 in the last octaves, where the offset has decayed by more than three decades.

6 Mechanism: direct path and relay

6.1 The decomposition

The offset at a given layer is built from the attention writes of the blocks below it. To see where the prompt’s imprint goes as it decays, we split each write into a direct part, in which the query reads the prompt, and a relay part, in which the query reads a continuation token that has already absorbed prompt information.

The write of attention block kk at query qq is ∑h∑jaq​jh​WOh​vjh\sum_{h}\sum_{j}a^{h}_{qj}W_{O}^{h}v^{h}_{j}, where hh runs over the heads of the block, aq​jha^{h}_{qj} is the attention weight of head hh from query qq to key jj, WOhW_{O}^{h} its output matrix and vjhv^{h}_{j} the value vector at key jj. Splitting keys into prompt tokens (direct) and continuation tokens (relay) and differencing the two prompts under the same continuation gives an exact decomposition of the attention contribution to the offset; sinks shared by both prompts (a common first token) cancel.

Table 6 reports the decomposition at three checkpoints. Five patterns stand out.

  • •

    Layer 1 has no relay, as it must: the continuation tokens are still identical after the first block, and the relay share is 0.020.02–0.030.03 at every checkpoint.

  • •

    At initialisation the late offset is 73–97% relay, rising with depth, and the relay component barely decays (αrelay\alpha_{\text{relay}} from 0.180.18 in layer 2 to 0.010.01 in layer 11), while the direct path decays as a uniform head would (αdirect≈0.68\alpha_{\text{direct}}\approx 0.68–0.700.70 in every layer, the layer-1 value). The long tail of untrained networks is relay.

  • •

    Training makes relay leak and steepens the direct path: at step 512 αrelay≈0.38\alpha_{\text{relay}}\approx 0.38–0.520.52 and αdirect≈0.82\alpha_{\text{direct}}\approx 0.82–0.960.96 in layers 2–11, while relay still dominates the late offset (0.550.55–0.880.88).

  • •

    After training the components no longer add up simply: in layers 6–11 αdirect≈0.39\alpha_{\text{direct}}\approx 0.39–0.410.41 and αrelay≈0.19\alpha_{\text{relay}}\approx 0.19–0.230.23, yet their sum decays with α≈0.61\alpha\approx 0.61–0.630.63. The two components have different decay rates and a cross term (they are anti-aligned at late times), so the exponent of the sum cannot be read off the exponents of the parts. The same happened on hand-written scenes from step ∼\sim4000 on. Part of it is bookkeeping (softmax weights sum to one, so attention moved off the prompt lands on the continuation); in this regime only the sum is reliable.

  • •

    Attention weights mislead. Raw (or value-weighted) attention to the prompt predicts α\alpha only around steps 512–1000; before, it misses relay; after, sinks (token 0 and in-prompt delimiters) dominate the weights while carrying no prompt-specific information.

These patterns describe the mechanism at a fixed checkpoint. We now ask when the mechanism appears during training.

6.2 When forgetting appears in training

Table 7 and Figure 5 follow the same 400 prompt pairs through training. Three phases appear.

  • •

    Onset (steps 128–512, roughly 0.3–1B tokens). Up to step 128 the exponents are those of the untrained network, and so is the attention: normalised entropy ≥0.95\geq 0.95 in every layer measured. Between steps 128 and 512 every layer from 2 on jumps (layer 11: 0.41→0.52→0.680.41\to 0.52\to 0.68); the path decomposition at step 512 shows that this is relay starting to leak (Table 6). Attention leaves the uniform regime at the same time: the normalised entropy falls from 0.980.98 to 0.850.85 and 0.650.65 in layer 3 and from 0.950.95 to 0.680.68 and 0.540.54 in layer 12 between steps 128, 256 and 512, while layer 1 stays at 0.980.98. Forgetting is strongest at step 512 and relaxes slightly afterwards in the deep layers.

  • •

    First-layer locality (steps 1000–4000). Layer 1 keeps the uniform-head value 0.720.72–0.730.73 until step 1000 and reaches 0.960.96 by step 4000: the first block becomes recency-biased only after forgetting in deeper layers is established, and its attention entropy falls only then (0.980.98 at step 1000, 0.820.82 at step 4000). On the same 400 pairs, the attention mass on token 0 stays at or below 0.0030.003 in every layer measured (1, 2, 3, 7, 12) up to step 1000 and appears only afterwards (0.0310.031 in layer 7 at step 4000, 0.0710.071 at 16000, 0.0890.089 at the end; 0.050.05–0.100.10 in layers 5–11 of the final model).

  • •

    Settling. By the end of training deep layers sit at 0.580.58–0.660.66, and the depth dependence of the untrained network (0.73→0.360.73\to 0.36 from layer 1 to 11) has given way to a profile that is roughly flat beyond layer 3.

Forgetting therefore sets in between steps 128 and 512, earlier than the formation of attention sinks and earlier than the first layer becoming strongly recency-biased. The earliest change observed in training is that relay begins to leak, while layer 1, where only the direct path exists, stays in the untrained regime until step 1000.

7 Causal test: compensating dilution

7.1 The intervention

The decomposition of Section 6 shows that the prompt’s imprint decays through dilution, but it is a measurement, not an intervention. To test whether dilution is the cause of the decay, we cancel it.

We add γ​log⁡q+1P\gamma\log\frac{q+1}{P} to the logits from continuation queries qq to prompt tokens 1..P−11..P-1, either uniformly (γ=1\gamma=1) or with per-head γl,h\gamma_{l,h} fitted so that each head’s attention to a typical prompt token stops decaying. The boost exactly compensates the 1/t1/t shrinkage of the prompt’s share of attention under uniform attention.

7.2 What the intervention removes

Table 8 shows that compensating dilution removes forgetting at initialisation and at step 512; after training, uniform compensation leaves α=0.11\alpha=0.11–0.290.29 and per-head compensation reverses the decay. Under uniform compensation the residual α\alpha matched the residual slope of prompt attention in a preliminary run on three hand-written scenes (steps 0, 256, 512: residual α=0.06\alpha=0.06–0.080.08, 0.140.14–0.150.15, 0.230.23–0.280.28 against residual attention slopes 0.090.09, 0.160.16, 0.260.26); per-head compensation brings α\alpha to 0.050.05–0.130.13 at steps 0 and 512, and overshoots after training (α<0\alpha<0: the prompt’s influence grows), where the attention-based calibration does not converge, a sign that the attention a head pays to the prompt is not the same as the information it carries.

7.3 What the test does and does not show

Per-head compensation raises perplexity by 140%140\% or more (Section 9), so the compensated network runs far from its training distribution. The test therefore shows that, in these networks, the forgetting we measure disappears once dilution is compensated: dilution is necessary for it. It does not show that the compensated network computes as the original one does, and it does not show that dilution is sufficient on its own; that it is sufficient is shown by the untrained networks and the linear relay model of Section 4.5, where uniform attention alone produces the decay. Within this caveat, no second forgetting mechanism is needed.

In a preliminary run on the hand-written scenes, continuations generated by the model from the prompt gave the same α\alpha as human-written ones (within 0.10.1; identical early in training), so the rate of forgetting is not inherited from the statistics of the model’s own text; all real-corpus results above use human-written continuations.

8 Exterior: what survives in the generated text

The question.

So far the continuation has been written by a human, so the exterior was the same for both prompts. In free generation the exterior is itself a product of the model, and the prompt can influence later tokens only through the text it has already caused. What properties of the prompt can still be read off from that text?

The probe.

The observer sees only text: a window of generated tokens ending at tt (3232 tokens for Qwen, 88 for Pythia) is turned into a hashed unigram histogram (40964096 bins, square-root normalised), and a logistic-regression probe (inputs standardised, projected on 1616 principal components, L2L_{2} penalty C=0.1C=0.1) tells the two prompts of a pair apart under 5-fold stratified cross-validation. The numbers are accuracies averaged over three scenes, with 3232 freely generated trajectories per prompt (pure sampling at temperature 11). Chance is 0.50.5; the 95th percentile of a null obtained by splitting one prompt’s trajectories at random is 0.580.58–0.630.63. These runs predate the main pipeline and use three hand-written scenes (Chinese for Qwen, English with a French language variant for Pythia).

What survives.

Details, paraphrase and genre become undecodable from the text, while language remains decodable (0.810.81 for Qwen2.5-0.5B, 0.840.84 for Pythia-160m at t=512t=512). Language is not conserved: in Qwen, 4–11 of 32 trajectories per scene switch language, mostly towards Chinese, the model’s dominant mode. The teacher-forced offset for the language axis still decays (α=0.54\alpha=0.54–0.650.65 in layers 3–11 of trained Pythia-160m, against 0.610.61–0.690.69 for a one-word detail; Table 3), so language survives through the trajectory itself, not through memory of the prompt.

Why language survives.

The two observations are complementary rather than contradictory. Corollary 1 concerns the sensitivity of the next-token distribution to the prompt given the same history; in free generation the history is itself a function of the prompt. Language therefore survives along an exterior channel: the prompt tilts the first tokens towards its language, and every later token is predicted from a history already written in that language, which keeps the trajectory there until it switches by chance. This is precisely the sense of the analogy: what persists is what the exterior field carries.

9 Application: a dilution knob, and its costs

The analysis above says that the prompt’s imprint fades because its share of attention shrinks as 1/t1/t. This suggests a simple intervention: boost the logits from the prompt by a factor that cancels the shrinkage, and see whether forgetting slows. We test this on Pythia-160m with a uniform boost s​log⁡q+1Ps\log\frac{q+1}{P} on the prompt, and compare it with a placebo of the same mean strength applied to the start of the continuation.

9.1 The trade-off

  • •

    A mild boost is cheap: s=0.5s=0.5 lowers α\alpha by 0.170.17–0.250.25 for +2.6%+2.6\% perplexity. The placebo also lowers α\alpha, because the boosted continuation tokens follow the prompt directly and already carry its imprint through relay. At matched retention the prompt boost is much cheaper than the placebo (αL11≈0.5\alpha_{\text{L11}}\approx 0.5: +2.6%+2.6\% at s=0.5s=0.5 vs. +10.3%+10.3\% at s=1s=1). At matched strength it is costlier on these pairs (+16.1%+16.1\% vs. +10.3%+10.3\% at s=1s=1), whereas in a preliminary run on three hand-written scenes, whose continuations were generated from the prompt, the two cost about the same (s=0.5s=0.5: +2.7%+2.7\% vs. +2.2%+2.2\% on human-written text, +1.3%+1.3\% vs. +1.7%+1.7\% on the model’s own text; s=1s=1: +14.0%+14.0\% vs. +14.8%+14.8\% and +8.3%+8.3\% vs. +10.8%+10.8\%). The cost of remembering the prompt thus depends on its relevance to the continuation: here the WikiText continuations are unrelated to the prompt, and attending to it more hurts prediction.

  • •

    Per-head calibrated compensation is too strong to be practical (+140% to +376% perplexity).

9.2 Instruction adherence and its side effects

  • •

    Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, system prompt “answer only in French”, 2048 generated tokens: share of samples fully in French 31%→94%31\%\to 94\% at s=0.5s=0.5. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: 84%→9484\%\to 94–100%100\% for all boosts; a constant boost with the same mean bias does as well, with less echo.

  • •

    Multi-turn conversation (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, 8 turns, English user turns asking for the next chapter, natural reply endings, 32 conversations per condition). Without boost the French share drops from 0.900.90 to 0.810.81–0.870.87 after the first turn and 78% of conversations stay in French throughout. With log⁡t\log t boosts of strength 0.10.1 and 0.250.25: last-three-turn French share 0.900.90 and 0.960.96, conversations fully in French 84% and 91%. Constant boosts with the same mean bias: 0.940.94 and 0.940.94, 84% and 88%. Echo in late turns stays at the baseline level (the excess is concentrated in the first reply, more so for the constant boost: 12.912.9 vs. 8.68.6 leak words per 1000 at the higher strength); repetition does not increase; replies are about 10% shorter. With 32 conversations per condition these differences are trends rather than significant effects, and the log⁡t\log t shape shows no clear advantage over a matched constant: the benefit comes from extra attention to the system prompt.

  • •

    Instruction echo. With forced-length single-turn generation, the share of outputs whose second half talks about the instruction rises from 19% to 56–69% (1.5B); much of this text is filler written after the story has ended.

Across all three tests, the pattern is the same: what helps is extra attention to the instruction, not the shape of the correction.

10 Discussion and conclusion

A transformer’s memory of its prompt, measured as the prompt-induced offset of the hidden state under a shared continuation, decays approximately as a power law whose exponent we can measure, bound and manipulate. The bound follows from geometric dilution of attention and the number of relay rounds through depth; it is attained asymptotically in the uniform-attention regime, whose exact solution with one gain per layer accounts for the slow, depth-dependent forgetting of untrained networks; trained networks suppress relay within the first billion training tokens, before attention sinks form, and come close to pure dilution. Compensating the dilution removes or reverses forgetting, so dilution is necessary for it in these networks; that it is also sufficient is shown by the untrained networks and the linear relay model, where uniform attention alone produces the decay. Two negative results matter as much: attention weights are not a reliable measurement of the effect, and a log⁡t\log t-shaped compensation is no better than a constant boost for keeping an instruction alive; what helps is extra attention to the instruction, not the shape of the correction.

These findings come with limitations. The constant of Theorem 1 can grow exponentially with depth and the bound is informative only for t≫P​e2​Bt\gg Pe^{2B}, so the theorem constrains the asymptotic shape of the decay rather than the exponents we fit; the non-degeneracy assumption is verified empirically rather than derived, with a small margin in the first block of Qwen. The core measurements stop at Pythia-1b and the behavioural tests at Qwen2.5-1.5B, so we cannot exclude changes at larger scale, although the agreement of the untrained 160m, 410m and 1b models and of the trained Pythia and Qwen models gives no hint of one. Prompts are English (with French and, in preliminary runs, Chinese variants), and all free generations use a single temperature. Continuations are WikiText passages, contiguous or as shuffled sentences; the shape of the trained decay depends on which (Section 5.5), and in trained Qwen the late slowdown is an oscillation of layer-1 attention around 1/t1/t whose period, and its relation to the rotary frequencies, remain open. The single-turn behavioural test forces a fixed generation length, so its late text partly consists of filler written after the story has ended; the multi-turn test avoids this but has only 32 conversations per condition. Exponents are fitted over at most seven octaves, which does not allow the logarithmic and small-gain descriptions of the untrained curves to be told apart.

Several questions are left open. The most direct is scale: whether the exponents we fit stay in the same range at larger models, and whether the depth dependence of untrained networks survives. A second is the period of the layer-1 oscillation in Qwen, which we have not tied to the rotary frequencies. A third is whether the picture changes under instruction tuning: all our trained models are pretrained only, and the path decomposition across checkpoints suggests that the training process itself is what suppresses relay, so a model trained on dialogue may forget its system prompt at a different rate. Finally, the toolkit we release makes it easy to measure α\alpha on any Hugging Face model, and we hope the community will extend the measurements beyond the range we could afford.

Conditional on the generated text the prompt is forgotten; what survives, such as the language of the conversation, is carried by the text itself.

A.2 Constants of a multi-head block

An attention block with HH heads writes ∑h=1HWO(h)​∑jai​j(h)​WV(h)​LN​(hj)\sum_{h=1}^{H}W_{O}^{(h)}\sum_{j}a^{(h)}_{ij}W_{V}^{(h)}\mathrm{LN}(h_{j}), where HH is the number of heads, ai​j(h)a^{(h)}_{ij} are the attention weights of head hh, WV(h)W_{V}^{(h)} its value matrix, and WO(h)W_{O}^{(h)} the block of columns of WOW_{O} that reads head hh. For each head let

Bh=d​‖WQ(h)‖​‖WK(h)‖dh+βh,Vh=d​‖WO(h)​WV(h)‖,ρh=2​dr​‖WO(h)​WV(h)‖,λh=2​d​‖WQ(h)‖​‖WK(h)‖r​dh,B_{h}=\frac{d\,\|W_{Q}^{(h)}\|\,\|W_{K}^{(h)}\|}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}+\beta_{h},\quad V_{h}=\sqrt{d}\,\|W_{O}^{(h)}W_{V}^{(h)}\|,\quad\rho_{h}=\frac{2\sqrt{d}}{r}\|W_{O}^{(h)}W_{V}^{(h)}\|,\quad\lambda_{h}=\frac{2d\,\|W_{Q}^{(h)}\|\,\|W_{K}^{(h)}\|}{r\sqrt{d_{h}}},

with βh\beta_{h} the contribution of query and key biases, if any. The constants of Section 4 are to be read as

B=maxh⁡Bh,V=∑hVh,ρ=∑hρh,λ​V:=∑hλh​Vh,B=\max_{h}B_{h},\qquad V=\sum_{h}V_{h},\qquad\rho=\sum_{h}\rho_{h},\qquad\lambda V:=\sum_{h}\lambda_{h}V_{h},

so that every bound proved for one head with (Bh,Vh,ρh,λh)(B_{h},V_{h},\rho_{h},\lambda_{h}) sums over heads into the same bound with (B,V,ρ,λ​V)(B,V,\rho,\lambda V); in particular K1,K2,K3K_{1},K_{2},K_{3} of Lemma 3 carry no hidden factor HH. Gains of the normalisation layers are absorbed into the adjacent weight matrices. Lemma 1 then holds head by head with these constants, by the same arguments.

A.3 Positions

Lemma 5.

With rotary position encodings, the logit between a query at continuation distance ii and a key at continuation distance j≤ij\leq i depends on the positions only through i−ji-j; in particular it is the same function of (hl−1​(i),hl−1​(j))(h_{l-1}(i),h_{l-1}(j)) in both runs, whatever the prompt lengths PP and P′P^{\prime}.

Proof.

Rotary encodings give s=⟨Rp​q,Rp′​k⟩/dh=⟨q,Rp′−p​k⟩/dhs=\langle R_{p}q,R_{p^{\prime}}k\rangle/\sqrt{d_{h}}=\langle q,R_{p^{\prime}-p}k\rangle/\sqrt{d_{h}} because RpR_{p} is orthogonal and Rp⊤​Rp′=Rp′−pR_{p}^{\top}R_{p^{\prime}}=R_{p^{\prime}-p}, where qq and kk are the query and key vectors, p,p′p,p^{\prime} their absolute positions and RpR_{p} the rotary matrix at position pp. A continuation token at distance jj sits at absolute position P+jP+j in one run and P′+jP^{\prime}+j in the other, so p′−p=j−ip^{\prime}-p=j-i in both. Positions enter nowhere else in the block. ∎

With absolute position embeddings the continuation tokens would carry different embeddings in the two runs; we then take P=P′P=P^{\prime}, which restores δ0≡0\delta_{0}\equiv 0 at continuation positions.

Scope.

The proof covers multi-head attention with full or partial rotary encodings or with no positional term in the logits, grouped-query attention (key and value matrices shared across heads only change the per-head constants), query and key biases, LayerNorm and RMSNorm, and sequential or parallel blocks; absolute position embeddings are covered for P=P′P=P^{\prime}. It does not cover additive position biases that grow with distance, such as ALiBi: they make the logits unbounded, so Lemma 1(a) fails, even though they push towards more forgetting rather than less; nor logit scalings that grow with context length, such as Scalable-Softmax [Nakanishi, 2025], which also make the logits unbounded and, unlike ALiBi, can push towards less forgetting; nor sliding-window attention, for which the number of visible keys stops growing and the dilution lemma no longer applies as stated; nor non-softmax attention.

The weights wk∝zk−1/(k!​(k−1)!)w_{k}\propto z^{k-1}/\big(k!(k-1)!\big), z=G​uz=Gu, are those of the series of I1​(2​z)I_{1}(2\sqrt{z}); for z≫1z\gg 1 they concentrate around k≈zk\approx\sqrt{z} (the mean of k−1k-1 is ζ(z)=z−34+O(z−1/2)\zeta(z)=\sqrt{z}-\frac{3}{4}+O(z^{-1/2}), from (9)), so m1≈zm_{1}\approx\sqrt{z} and m2≈zm_{2}\approx z. The relative error of the small-gain form is then of order

Ql​u2​Gl+1P​Glu+Gl2​P+τ,\frac{Q_{l}u}{2G_{l}}\;+\;\frac{1}{P}\sqrt{\frac{G_{l}}{u}}\;+\;\frac{G_{l}}{2P}\;+\;\tau,

For z≲1z\lesssim 1, as in the first layers of our measurements, w1w_{1} dominates and all corrections are small, but the asymptotic expansion (9) of the local exponent is not valid there; this is why the fitted GlG_{l} of Section 4.5 are effective parameters. Statements (a) and (b) of Corollary 2 are properties of φ\varphi; a bound on δ\delta such as the one above does not by itself bound its logarithmic derivative, so the local exponents of the model are covered by (a) and (b) only to the extent that δ\delta is well approximated by φ\varphi uniformly over an octave.

Appendix B Non-degeneracy of pre-norm activations

Table 10 reports ‖Π​h‖/d\|\Pi h\|/\sqrt{d} at the input of every block and of the final norm, over 80 sequences of length T=1024T=1024 (40 real-corpus prompts ×\times 2 WikiText continuations). The minimum is never close to zero on these sequences; this supports Assumption 1 empirically but does not prove it for other continuations or longer contexts. The embeddings (block 0 input) are small but are not used by Theorem 1 (Assumption 1). For the trained Pythia-1b the minimum over blocks 1–15 is 0.490.49 (median 0.570.57–2.812.81) and 0.970.97 at the final norm, again a wide margin. Qwen2.5-0.5B uses RMSNorm (Π=I\Pi=I); its minimum over block inputs 1–23 is 0.1050.105 (median 0.170.17–2.562.56) and 1.301.30 at the final norm. Because its blocks are sequential, the post-attention norms enter Assumption 1 as well; their minimum is 0.0120.012, in the first block, so r/d=0.012r/\sqrt{d}=0.012 for this model.

Appendix D Toolkit

The code runs on a single laptop and measures, for any Hugging Face causal language model: the prompt offset under shared continuations and its signal, noise and mean-squared versions, with the unbiased estimator, centre-labelled octave windows, global and local exponents, and bootstrap intervals over prompt pairs (real_run.py; scale_run.py for the hand-written scenes); the non-degeneracy check of Assumption 1 (prenorm_check.py); the exact direct/relay decomposition of the attention writes together with uniform and per-head dilution compensation (real_mech.py); the trade-off between retention and perplexity with a placebo control (tradeoff_real.py); and the single- and multi-turn instruction-adherence tests (behavior_test.py, multiturn_test.py). The toolkit, together with the exact real-corpus prompt pairs, will be released publicly.
